contents.name: Definition 2.31: a framing of Y in M is a trivialization of the normal bundle nu
(2.32): inverse images of regular values give a framed bordism class, with the target-orientation caveat
(2.34): the Pontryagin-Thom collapse with a cutoff function, in the model S^q = R^q union infinity
Theorem 2.35: [M,S^q] to Omega^fr_{n;M} is an isomorphism independent of the choices
Definition 3.8: smooth homotopy and the set [M,N] of smooth homotopy classes
Theorem 3.9 proof, first half: phi is well defined by perturbing a homotopy to be transverse to a point, fixed near the ends
Well-definedness of psi: a framed bordism in Delta^1 x M gives a collapse map Delta^1 x M to S^q
The identity phi o psi = id
Lemma 3.12 with psi o phi = id: the cutoff homotopy and the equality of differentials along Y
Exercise 3.14: the two omitted details (cutoff function and the use of framing equality up to homotopy)
Exercise 3.15: Theorem 3.9 can fail for M noncompact
contents.reason: The commissioned fixed-codimension statement is only for closed sources, where the collapse and the compact complement are used; the noncompact failure is a recorded scope boundary and no item builds a noncompact variant.

contents.name: Exercise 3.16: framed links in S^3 and the computation of Omega^fr_{1;S^3}
Theorem 2.37 (Hopf): the oriented and mod-two degree classifications of maps M to S^m
contents.reason: The Hopf degree theorem is the commissioned subject of the planned later differential-topology page the-hopf-degree-theorem; it is not proved here, and the framed 0-manifold input it uses is supplied by this pair.

contents.name: Lemma 4.16: [S^m,S^q]_* = [S^m,S^q] for m,q >= 1, with the rotation and disk arguments
(4.42)-(4.43): the stabilization sequence Omega^fr_{n;S^m} and sigma prepending d/dx_1 to the normal framing
Theorem 4.44: sigma is an isomorphism for m >= 2n+2
contents.reason: The sharp stable range is Freudenthal's suspension theorem in the library's algebraic-topology supplier; the stable Pontryagin-Thom statement only needs the eventual isomorphism of the suspension system, which that page supplies.

contents.name: Exercise 4.46: the bound of Theorem 4.44 is optimal for n = 1
contents.reason: The optimality of the stable range is a refinement of the suspension theorem; the pair needs the eventual isomorphism only and does not study the sharp bound.

contents.name: (5.15)-(5.19): stable normal framings versus stable tangential framings
Proposition 5.21: the colimit of the stabilization sequence is the bordism group of stably framed manifolds
Corollary 5.22 (stable Pontryagin-Thom): pi^s_n is isomorphic to Omega^fr_n
(5.30)-(5.32): the equatorial sphere with the canonical normal framing and the unstable J-homomorphism
Exercise 5.34: the canonically normally framed equatorial sphere is null bordant
Exercise 5.35: low cases n=0 and n=1, m=2,3, including the non-nullhomotopic S^3 to S^2
(5.25)-(5.26): twists of a framing by a map Y to GL_q(R) and the deformation to orthonormal framings
(5.24): the ring structure on Omega^fr_* given by Cartesian product
contents.reason: The pair states the group isomorphism and the disjoint-union structure needed by the fixed-codimension and stable statements; the multiplicative ring structure is used only by the later characteristic-number and signature pages and is not commissioned here.

sources.title: John Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint (Princeton University Press)
sources.locator: Chapter 7, 'Framed cobordism; the Pontryagin construction', printed pp. 42-51, including Lemmas 1-4, the Product Neighborhood Theorem, the proofs of Theorems A-C, the remarks on boundaries and the Hopf theorem, and Problem 17; complete scanned text fetched

contents.name: Framing of a submanifold N in M as a basis of the normal space at each point
Definition of framed cobordism of framed submanifolds
Statement that framed cobordism is an equivalence relation
Definition of the Pontryagin manifold (f^{-1}(y), f_*b) from a regular value and a positive basis
Theorem A: different regular values and positive bases give framed-cobordant Pontryagin manifolds
Theorem B: two maps are smoothly homotopic if and only if their Pontryagin manifolds are framed cobordant
Theorem C: every compact framed submanifold occurs as a Pontryagin manifold
Lemma 1: two positive bases at a regular value give framed-cobordant Pontryagin manifolds
Lemma 2: a sufficiently close regular value gives a framed-cobordant Pontryagin manifold
Product Neighborhood Theorem for a framed submanifold (compact, boundaryless)
Proof of Theorem C via a product representation and a radial model map R^p to S^p
Lemma 4: maps with a common regular value and the same induced framing are smoothly homotopic
Proof of Theorem B: a framed cobordism constructs a homotopy and Lemma 4 compares the ends
Remark: the theory generalizes to manifolds with boundary using maps carrying the boundary to a base point; the cohomotopy group and union of submanifolds
Application: the Hopf theorem for connected oriented M, and the mod-two theorem for nonorientable M
contents.reason: The Hopf classification is the commissioned subject of the later differential-topology page the-hopf-degree-theorem; the framed-zero-manifold computation it consumes is scaffolded here, and no Hopf theorem item is minted on this pair.

contents.name: Remark: Pontryagin's classification of framed 1-manifolds in S^m for m = p+1 >= 4
Problem 17: Omega^fr(M) as framed cobordism classes with the union operation

contents.name: Definition 6.1 and Proposition 6.3: cobordism of closed manifolds is an equivalence relation
Definitions 6.4-6.5: cobordism groups; Example 6.7: the inverse image of a regular value is a framed manifold
Pontryagin-Thom construction 6.8: collapse of the exterior of a tubular neighbourhood to the Thom space
Example 6.9: the Pontryagin-Thom map of S^0 in S^n and the pinch class (1,1)
6.10: B_m(N,X,eta) = [N,T(eta)] with the two inverse constructions
Definition 6.11 and Example 6.12: degree and the signed local-sum formula
Proposition 6.13 (Hopf): B_0(N,{*},epsilon^n) = [N,S^n] = Z by degree
Definition 6.14: a framing of M^m is an embedding M in S^{m+k} together with a framing of the normal bundle
Definition 6.16: the framed cobordism ring, addition by disjoint union
Theorem 6.17: Omega^fr_m = pi^S_m via lim B_m(S^{m+k},{*},epsilon^k) = lim pi_{m+k}(S^k)
Proposition 6.18: the J-homomorphism sends a homotopy class to the framed sphere with its standard framing
Remark 6.19: framed cobordism questions for homotopy spheres and the surgery obstruction
contents.reason: The surgery classification of homotopy spheres belongs to the later surgery and h-cobordism pages of the track; this pair supplies only the framed cobordism input and does not mint surgery theory.

contents.name: 3.1-3.3: manifolds with boundary and cobordism classes of closed manifolds forming the cobordism groups
3.5-3.7: the normal bundle of an embedding, the tubular neighbourhood theorem and the neighbourhood-retract corollary
3.8-3.9: the Thom space as a one-point compactification and as the collapse of the exterior of the epsilon-neighbourhood
3.10-3.11: differentiable approximation on a closed set, Euclidean-valued and manifold-valued
3.12: a sufficiently close approximation is homotopic to the original map
3.13-3.14: construction of lambda: pi_{n+k}(T(xi),infinity) to the cobordism group and its well-definedness through transverse approximations and compact neat preimages
3.15: lambda is surjective for the universal bundle, via the explicit collapse p_4 p_3 p_2 p_1
3.16: lambda is injective, by deforming the map to a bundle map near the inverse image
